facts.claim: "Nobody" is the first of three tracks on the digital single 'Live from Dogtown Studio' by The Crane Wives, released April 3, 2023. The other two tracks are "Queen of Nothing" and "The Wolf".
Streaming credits list all four band members as composers of "Nobody": Katherine Rose Pillsbury, Emilee Jade Petersmark, Daniel Bryan Rickabus and Benjamin Allen Zito.

The band shared a Patreon post titled 'Nobody - The Crane Wives (Live from Dogtown Studios)' on Feb 16, 2023. It said they had a great time recording at Dogtown Studios and wanted patrons to see the videos before they reached streaming services.
The band's own announcement said new Dogtown Session videos of "Queen of Nothing", "Nobody" and "The Wolf" were out.
The song was already in the band's live set. A live version (4:19) appears on the live album 'Here I Am', recorded at the Listening Room in Grand Rapids on Feb 28, 2020 and released Oct 14, 2020.

Credits for 'Here I Am' list Petersmark (vocals, guitar), Pillsbury (vocals, guitar), Zito (bass) and Rickabus (drums, vocals). The album was produced by the Crane Wives, with live mixing and engineering by Nicholas Connor Jones.

A Washington Square News concert review says the band opened a 2023 New York show with "Nobody", with Petersmark carrying the vocals. The review describes the song as depicting a toxic relationship with another woman.
A Medium piece on queer folk artists describes "Nobody" as a toxic queer love anthem. It says Petersmark is openly queer and that her experience is embedded in the band's songs.

The Crane Wives formed in Grand Rapids, Michigan in 2010. Petersmark and Pillsbury started out working at a Chinese restaurant in Grandville, and the name nods to The Decemberists' album The Crane Wife.

The band is Emilee Petersmark, Kate Pillsbury, Dan Rickabus and Ben Zito. They use three-part vocal harmonies and eclectic instrumentation. Their studio albums are Safe Ship, Harbored, The Fool in Her Wedding Gown, Coyote Stories, Foxlore and Beyond Beyond Beyond (2024).

research.lineage: The band is a Grand Rapids, Michigan indie rock and folk act whose three-part harmonies and folk influence set them apart in a scene dominated by indie rock.

draft:
The whole song turns on four words at the end of the chorus. **Nobody** keeps circling one claim, that no one has ever loved the narrator the way this woman does, and then it lands on the catch: "Like she tells me she does." The love is real enough to name. Whether it's love or just her word for it, the narrator can't say. On the second pass the line slips to "So she tells me," and near the end it tries "Like she loves me" before falling back to the hedge. You can hear someone trying out the sentence they want to believe, and failing to hold it.

The verses build the woman out of opposites. She's soft-spoken as a spider, her voice swings like a hatchet through the trees, and she lights cigarettes like lanterns against the dark in the narrator's head. Then comes the line that holds the whole relationship: "Tender as a bruise, sharper than a razor." A bruise is tender because something hurt it. The comfort and the injury come from the same place, and the narrator can't pull them apart. Her storm is the only one the narrator has ever known, which is the saddest admission here. There's nothing to compare it to.

Then the bridge, where the song stops describing and starts arguing with itself. Something is better than nothing, isn't it, isn't it, isn't it. The repetition is a person talking themselves into staying. "What does it hurt, a little bit?" gets asked and half-answered, and the answer trails off into the same words said again and again. Gratitude and fear sit in the same breath, and the song won't choose between them.

The Crane Wives, a Grand Rapids band whose folk leanings and three-part harmonies set them apart in a mostly indie-rock scene, all share writing credit on the song. It isn't new to them. A version appears on their 2020 live album *Here I Am*, and they opened a 2023 New York show with it, Emilee Petersmark carrying the vocal. Critics have heard it as a toxic love song between two women, and Petersmark is openly queer. This Dogtown Studio take was shared with the band's patrons as a video before it went to streaming services.

The arrangement keeps a steady hand under all that unease. Strummed acoustic guitar and bass hold a driving, mid-tempo groove, the drums push on the snare, and an electric guitar threads a melodic line through the middle. The lead voice is clear and direct. When the harmony voices come in, the sound fills out, and the claim at the center starts to sound like more than one person repeating it.

It sticks because the hook is a lie the narrator almost believes, and singing along makes you almost believe it too.
